item.title: Volkswagen’s replacement for the ID.4 crossover is here
item.description:
The new EV’s digital cockpit can mimic instrument displays from VWs of old.

Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossoverdebuted in 2021, one of VW’s first new electric vehicles designed in the wake ofdieselgate. A year later, the companybegan local productionin Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unitin the process. But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4earlier this year. And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.

Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.

VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.

Alongside the mainstream name, it has a more mainstream look, though it’s part of VW’s new design language. For those keeping track of thevariousinterestingnamescar companies give their design languages—it can’t just be me—this one is called Pure Positive. The automaker says it wants the ID. Tiguan to feel like it belongs to the premium rather than mainstream segment, both inside and out.

Based on the images VW supplied to Ars, I think they’ve mostly met that brief; the R-Line interior in particular looks rather good to me. More importantly though, VW has been listening to feedback.

The return to normal door handles will be welcome, even if it might have been driven byChinese vehicle regulators. Even more welcome are the plethora of physical controls: real buttons on the steering wheel, real switches for the climate control and windows, and real physical air vents, not computer-controlled ones. There’s a new 15-inch infotainment screen that looks nice but will need to be responsive, plus the option of a 12-inch passenger display, a trend I continue to bemoan likeGrandpa Simpson shouting at the clouds.

One feature that really got my attention is one of the options for the new 10-inch digital main instrument display: the retro dials. Instead of something presumably 21st-century looking—I don’t know since we didn’t get any press shots of the default theme—you can opt to replicate the dials and warning lights from an Mk1 Golf, an Mk2 Golf Country, an Mk 4 Golf, a first-gen Tiguan, a racing Toureg, or the Beetle. (I’m not sure if it’s the original rear-engined Beetle or the retro one designed by J Mays in the late 1990s.)

Pre-sales for the electric Tiguan start in Europe next week, with a starting price in Germany of 42,695 euros ($44,716). Although the ID. Tiguan is coming to the US, VW told us it “has not announced North American timing for the vehicle. Following the European ID. Tiguan launch in early 2027, the company will share North American timing, offer structure, pricing, and other market-specific details in due course.”

item.title: Rocket Report: A rare Falcon 9 scrub; is it just about Vulcan’s time to shine?
item.description:
“I can say we’re weeks away from launching on Vulcan.”

Welcome to Edition 9.14 of the Rocket Report! The big news this week, from our perspective, is that United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket appears to be close to launching. We’ve seen a no-earlier-than launch date for the return to flight mission of October 29 (an Amazon Leo flight), and the next rocket up after that, also an Amazon Leo mission, is also planned for this year. Assuming the solid rocket boosters work, Vulcan could be poised for a major breakthrough next year in cadence.

As always, wewelcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

Nuri rocket notches another success. South Korea successfully deployed five satellites for its first domestically launched microsatellite constellation during the fifth flight of its homegrown Nuri rocket Wednesday,Yonhap News Agency reports. In addition to the primary payload of five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety microsatellites, nine of the rocket’s 10 CubeSat secondary payloads were released as planned, according to the Korea AeroSpace Administration. PERSAT-02, developed by South Korean startup Quaternion, failed to separate from the rocket.

Pushing for more commercial activity… The mission was Nuri’s fourth consecutive success after its debut flight failed in 2021, raising the small-lift rocket’s overall launch success rate to 80 percent. After the launch, Science Minister Bae Kyung-hoon pledged continued government support for additional launches led by the private sector as South Korea seeks to shift from a government-led space development model toward a more commercially driven industry.

HyImpulse test flight slips into 2027. German launch startup HyImpulse has pushed the second flight of its SR75 suborbital rocket into spring 2027,European Spaceflight reports. As recently as last month, the company had said the flight would occur at the “end of 2026.” HyImpulse said the new target was based on its assessment of the remaining activities required under the license framework and the seasonal weather conditions at SaxaVord, rather than on the vehicle’s readiness.

This will be the rocket’s first flight from European soil… The flight from SaxaVord will be HyImpulse’s second SR75 mission and its first to carry commercial payloads. The company completed an initial test flight of the suborbital rocket on May 3, 2024, from the Koonibba Test Range in South Australia.

German launch company gets a new CEO. The Supervisory Board of Rocket Factory Augburg has appointed Alexander Dahm as CEO. He succeeds Indulis Kalnins and will be responsible for the company’s continued development and its path to the debut flight of the RFA ONE launch vehicle,the company said this week. Dahm has 30 years of aerospace experience, including involvement with the Ariane 5 program.

Still seeking orbit… “I am impressed by the grit, innovative strength, and passion with which a new generation of European launch vehicles is being developed here. Together, we will reach the next important milestones on the way to the maiden flight of RFA ONE and actively shape the company’s future,” Dahm said. RFA has been working toward its first orbital launch following the loss of its first stage during a 2024 static-fire test.

SpaceX has rare scrub of Falcon 9 late in countdown. A Falcon 9 launch planned for early Monday morning was scrubbed in the final minute of the count as the rocket was shifting into its automated startup sequence,Spaceflight Now reports. SpaceX didn’t provide a reason for the abort. The rocket is intended to launch a new batch of data satellites to low Earth orbit on behalf of the United States Space Force’s Space Development Agency.

A relatively young booster… The company targeted Tuesday, October 6, for its next launch attempt, but waved off that opportunity as well. Following additional changes, the company is now aiming for no earlier than Saturday, October 10. The mission will use Falcon 9 first stage booster B1103. This will be its sixth flight following the launches of the SDA’s T1TL-E, NROL-179, and three batches of Starlink satellites.

Europe’s progress on hop tests remains slow. The European Commission has extended the deadline for the SALTO reusable launcher project to the end of 2026, giving the program another three months to complete the first hop test of Europe’s Themis reusable rocket demonstrator,European Spaceflight reports. This is the latest in a series of extensions that have pushed the completion date back from the original November 2025 deadline.

A long wait… The ArianeGroup-led SALTO initiative is an 42.8 million euro EU research project that is part of the ESA-managed Themis program. SALTO comprises the first two low-altitude hop tests, with the aim of demonstrating that Themis can be launched, recovered, and then launched again. Themis arrived at Esrange, Sweden, in June 2025, following a two-week road journey from ArianeGroup’s Les Mureaux facility in France. It has since been doing something important while not launching or hopping, we presume.

Concerns about credit risks at SpaceX. SpaceX plans to raise $40 billion in debt to finance the purchase of Nvidia chips, andThe Financial Times reportsthat this has raised concerns about the large company’s creditworthiness. The publication reports that the spread on SpaceX’s five-year credit default swaps rose to 194 basis points on Wednesday, meaning it now costs $19,400 annually to protect $1 million of its debt against default.

Doubling down on Nvidia… As for the $40 billion in new debt, private capital firm Apollo was expected to lead the deal, while bond giant Pimco was among lenders in talks to fund it. It comes after the company issued $25 billion in investment-grade debt in June just weeks after raising $86 billion in its initial public offering. The new debt deal suggests SpaceX founder Elon Musk is doubling down on his bet on Nvidia’s technology.

Cape Canaveral to get drone protection. Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is getting lasers that can zap drones intruding into its airspace,TWZ reports. When installed, the new directed energy defense system will be part of a much larger effort to protect the spaceport against drone incursions. The idea is to ensure launch safety and keep prying eyes away from an installation full of secrets about America’s military and commercial space efforts.

Next step: sharks with laser beams?… Companies like SpaceX, United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Relativity Space use the installation for space launches. The base defense modernization effort comes as the Cape Canaveral region is inundated with drone incursions. There were hundreds last year. For the spaceport, lasers are even more important than for other locations needing drone protection. That’s because the traditional method of jamming radio frequencies to interfere with drone connections to controllers could damage space vehicles. (submitted by biokleen)

Vulcan stacking two launches for Amazon. In awide-ranging interview with Ars, Amazon Leo officials discussed their progress toward delivering an orbital broadband service to customers back on Earth. Among the challenges faced by the company was launch. “From day one we decided to go with a diverse set of partners to supply us with rockets,” Amazon Leo VP Rajeev Badyal said. “We started off with ULA, Blue Origin, Arianespace, and SpaceX. We signed deals with all four of them. We knew there was risk, but we had to get heavy lift vehicles.”

Vulcan on deck… Badyal said the company is currently working on back-to-back launches on Vulcan this year. “I can say we’re weeks away from launching on Vulcan,” he said. “Things are on track. We’ll follow that with an Arianespace launch and at least one more Vulcan this year. I can also tell you the infrastructure that we put and built with ULA now allows us to process two rockets simultaneously. So right now, there are two vehicle integration facilities, and both have a Vulcan rocket that is vertical and getting ready for our missions.”

Blue Origin building three more pads. Inan interview with Fox Newsthis week, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos said the company was going to construct three more launch pads after the rebuild of LC-36A to accommodate New Glenn. “We’re building three more pads,” Bezos said. “So we’re building—we’ll have a total of four pads that we’re under construction right now.” Bezos said this in the context of the company’s recent request to the FAA for 50 launches a year from Florida.

Bezos has much bigger goals long-term… “Our goal is to fly every day,” Bezos said. “And then once we’re flying every day, we want to fly every hour. And then once we’re flying every hour, we want to fly every minute. And by the way, that’s where I lose the team.” Bezos has long talked about making spaceflight routine, but launches every minute seems a tad ambitious for a company that has yet to launch once a month.

October 9: Long March 12 | Unknown payload | Wenchang Space Launch Site, China | 19:25 UTC

October 10: Falcon 9 | Tranche 1, Transport Layer A | Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. | 07:29 UTC

October 12: Falcon 9 | Starlink 15-25 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif. | 23:00 UTC

item.title: Microsoft barred from sponsoring foreign workers for US residency
item.description:
The US says Microsoft abused immigration rules; the company disputes the claim.

Donald Trump’s administration has temporarily banned Microsoft, Adobe, and several other tech companies from sponsoring workers for permanent US residency, claiming they abused immigration programs at the expense of American citizens.

Vice-president JD Vance said on Thursday that the H-1B visa programme for highly skilled foreign workers had “become rife with fraud” and that over-reliance on such schemes was “a fundamental insult to the American worker.”

He added that “no company in the US” had “abused this system” more than Microsoft.

Vance’s message to Microsoft that it could not “lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants” triggered an angry reaction from the Indian government.

“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the foreign ministry in New Delhi said in a statement on Friday.

Referring to Vance’s remarks, it said “such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem.”

Six other IT outsourcing companies—Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini—were also suspended from the Permanent Labor Certification, or Perm, program, which allows US employers to hire foreign workers on a permanent basis.

“Subpoenas have been served, investigations are under way and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Labor Department Inspector-General Anthony D’Esposito.

Microsoft said the “vast majority” of its employees in the US were American, while Tata Consultancy Services, India’s largest outsourcing company, said its strategy was centred on hiring locally in the US and that Perm applications were in “single digits in the last two years.”

Adobe and Tata as well as Cognizant, Infosys, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini did not respond to requests for comment.

The announcement marks the latest move in the Trump administration’s broad crackdown on immigration. It has previously taken aim at H-1B visas widely used by tech companies and specialist industries.

Last year, the White House attempted to impose a $100,000 fee on new applications, but, in June, a federal judge ruled the fee amounted to an unauthorized tax and infringed on Congress’ authority to raise funds. The Trump administration has appealed against the ruling.

Before the fee increase, the government charged $215 to register for the H-1B visa lottery and a $780 base fee for employers sponsoring visa applicants. More than 400,000 such visas were approved last year.

While Indians have been the biggest recipients of H-1B visas and the new restrictions target many of the largest outsourcing groups, the impact is likely to be small as the route from H-1B to permanent residency has been out of reach for most Indians, given a decades-long backlog.

Nearly 1 million people from India are waiting for employment-based permanent residency as of December last year, according to an August study by the non-profit National Foundation for American Policy.

Nasscom, the Indian IT services lobbying group, said the number of employees transitioning to permanent residency through Perm was “relatively limited” as Indian tech companies had “significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas.”

In his comments on Thursday, Vance said the visas were helping companies undercut US workers. He claimed some H-1B holders were earning between $20,000 and $48,000 less than US citizens hired for similar positions.

Amazon, the biggest user of H-1B visas, was not mentioned in the press conference. But Vance singled out Microsoft, saying it “laid off last year 6,000 American workers at the same time the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards,” referring to US permanent residency.

The White House on Thursday also announced a fraud investigation into the use of J-1 student visas at nine American universities, including Harvard, Yale, and Stanford.

Microsoft, whose shares dropped more than 1 percent following the announcement, said the visa applications mentioned by Vance were largely “to extend or change the status” of existing employees.

“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company said. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings.”

At a separate event on Thursday, the Trump administration gave Microsoft’s Indian-born chief executive, Satya Nadella, the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

He was honored alongside South African-born Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who was born in Taiwan.

Vance said there was no contradiction between the two announcements.

“Our message to Microsoft is: ‘You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.’”

Additional reporting by Michael Stott in New Delhi

item.title: Starlink spectrum deal boosts Musk plan to beat AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
item.description:
Nationwide 800 MHz spectrum to help Starlink provide mobile coverage indoors.

SpaceX has a deal to purchase nationwide low-band spectrum licenses for a planned terrestrial mobile network that would complement the space-based Starlink cellular service.

SpaceX will buy up to 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz bandfrom investment firm Grain Management, which bought the spectrum rights from T-Mobile earlier this year. T-Mobile had obtained the spectrum when it bought Sprint in 2020 and was required to sell the licenses under a merger condition imposed by the US government.

“This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US,”SpaceX said yesterday. SpaceX this week also received US approval to launch 15,000 satellites for an upgraded version of its mobile service that it says will be far more powerful than the current offering.

The 800 MHz spectrum licenses cover “approximately 100 percent of the US population,” the Federal Communications Commission said in a July 2026 orderapprovingGrain’s purchase of the T-Mobile licenses. While the licenses are nationwide, it’s not a huge amount of spectrum. It ranges from 4.85 megahertz to 14 megahertz depending on the county. The FCC said the 800 MHz spectrum can be used for terrestrial service, satellite-to-mobile service, or both.

SpaceX’s low-band purchase is in addition to 65 MHz of nationwide mid-band spectrum licenses it is buying from EchoStar. The FCC approved that $17 billion purchase in May 2026.

“While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings. Critically, most existing mobile devices already support this underused band,” SpaceX said.

SpaceX’s spectrum deal is likely to be approved by the FCC, but it could face opposition from small carriers. The Rural Wireless Associationopposed EchoStar’s spectrum salesto AT&T and SpaceX, saying the deals “continue the troubling pattern of spectrum aggregation that disadvantages rural wireless providers.” Across all carriers in the US, there isabout 1.1 GHzof licensed spectrum allocated to mobile operators, withthe big threeholding dominant spectrum portfolios.

SpaceX has beenclaiming for monthsthat Starlink Mobile will eventually offer better service than AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. SpaceX previously focused on partnering with carriers and providing them with satellite coverage for dead spots in their terrestrial networks. Stock prices for AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and satellite company AST SpaceMobile fell sharply today in response to SpaceX’s spectrum deal.

SpaceX’spartner for mobile servicein the US is T-Mobile, and the space company leased 10 MHz of nationwide mid-band spectrum from T-Mobile as part of that deal. With this week’s Grain deal, SpaceX is buying former T-Mobile spectrum in order to compete against the giant wireless carrier.

CEO Elon Musksaid in Augustthat Starlink would deploy many small base stations instead of “expensive and difficult-to-locate large cellular base stations.” He said the Starlink broadband antennas on the roofs of houses and businesses can help provide connectivity to cellphones.

SpaceX yesterdaysubmitted a filingthat asks the FCC to approve the low-band purchase. It said the deployment “will rely on radios feeding sectorized antennas on towers, rooftops, and other structures, configured to provide reliable signal coverage and meaningful broadband service. The propagation characteristics of 800 MHz (long-range coverage, strong performance against terrain and clutter, and superior building penetration) make this paired low-band spectrum an efficient coverage layer for markets of all sizes and densities, including areas where higher-frequency networks cannot serve.”

SpaceX has launched 650 Direct-to-Device satellites for its current mobile service and plans tolaunch up to 15,000next-generation satellites for a more powerful version. The FCCapproved the 15,000-satellite applicationon Tuesday.

“The V2 Starlink Mobile satellites will deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of our current generation, bringing high-speed service directly to unmodified devices anywhere in the world,” SpaceX said yesterday. “Additionally, the FCC authorized the full range of backhaul bands (in Ka/V/E/W) used by Starlink’s V3 broadband satellites, enabling them to operate with the existing Starlink gateway network.”

SpaceX said that once it deploys all its spectrum and launches next-generation satellites, it will be able to offer US residents “a reliable service indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between.” SpaceX previously told the Canadian government in afilingthat it “will begin launching its next-generation Starlink direct-to-device satellites with service beginning by late 2027,” and launch “thousands more satellites” by the end of 2028.

Terms of the SpaceX/Grain spectrum deal were not disclosed. Grain originally obtained the spectrum from T-Mobile in a swap that included cash and other spectrum licenses. Specifically, T-Mobile sold its 800 MHz spectrum licenses to Grain for $2.9 billion and Grain’s 600 MHz spectrum licenses that consist of 10 MHz in 212 counties covering approximately 15 percent of the US population.

“The 800 MHz licenses that Grain is acquiring (817–824 MHz paired with 862–869 MHz)—a valuable source of paired, broadband-ready, low-band spectrum—have been underutilized in recent years,” the FCC said in its approval of the cash-and-spectrum swap.

Dish was previously given the first option to buy the 800 MHz spectrum under a merger condition imposed by the US Department of Justice on T-Mobile’s purchase of Sprint. Dishdeclined the optionto buy it for $3.59 billion, and the offerexpiredin 2024, forcing T-Mobile to find a new buyer.

AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon are trying to counter SpaceX’s moves into mobile by pooling spectrum for a new joint venture focused on using satellite to cover dead zones in terrestrial networks. The big three carriersfinalized the joint venture agreementlast week, saying it will give other satellite operators a better chance to compete.

The venture will “improve the application and utilization of valuable and scarce nationally licensed spectrum resources,” the carriers said. They said they plan industry-wide device compatibility through a “standards-based approach to development involving operating system providers, mobile app developers and original equipment manufacturers.”

Existing carrier-satellite agreements will remain in place, and the three big carriers “can continue connectivity efforts independently,” the press release said. Meanwhile, anFCC planannounced this week could auction 25 MHz of mid-band spectrum for use in terrestrial and satellite networks.

The FCC alsoproposedrule changes that would allow 482 MHz of spectrum to be used for satellite-to-mobile service. This would be an expansion of the Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS) framework in which terrestrial wireless spectrum is made available for satellite use.

item.title: Your artwork could be featured in the next Debian release
item.description:
Debian Linux has put a call out for artist submissions for its next release: Forky.

The Debian Linux project has opened a call for community artwork submissions ahead of the release of the upcomingForky(Debian 14). If you think you’ve got the artistic chops, your art could appear on the boot screens, login prompts, and desktop wallpapers of millions of users. The submission deadline is November 26.

Continuing Debian’s community-driven ethos, the artwork submission process mirrors that of previous releases. The artwork must feel distinctively “Debian,” integrate cleanly without the need for core software patching, and remain visually appealing for the long term.

Elise Couper’s “Ceratopsian”theme was chosen as the winning default for Debian 13Trixie. For anyone who might not be up on the latest from the Toy Story franchise, the release names echo character names from the animated films.Trixiewas a triceratops introduced inToy Story 3, hence the “Ceratopsian” wink in the winning submission. It makes sense that the next version of Debian continues this trend with Forky, a character introduced in the franchise’s fourth entry. The Debian team cautions against overly busy designs that may cause user fatigue, but if anyone can successfully incorporateForky’s googly eyesinto the design somehow, know that you’d at least win the contest formyDebian desktop wallpaper.

Debian celebrated its 33rd anniversary in August 2026 and continues to position itself as the “universal operating system,” with support and compatibility stretching acrossdifferent hardware architectures. Debian’s latest point release, Trixie 13.7, arrived on September 12, 2026. Forky (Debian 14) is now in the later stages of its development cycle, with the artwork selection process marking one of the final boxes to be checked before the release is made available. Interested artists can review the submission requirementson the Debian Wiki.

item.title: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner
item.description:
New winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam for video of a roundworm and single-celled Dileptus.

Last monthwe coveredthe winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. Butallegations surfacedabout Xu’suse of AIwhile making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).

According to aBBC report,some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”

Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.

The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug (Cyerce kikutarobabai) on the move.

Here is Nikon’s full statement:

After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI. Nikon has adjusted the competition rankings on our website to reflect this decision.

This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent.

Advances in imaging and artificial intelligence continue to evolve rapidly, creating new challenges for organizations across many fields. This event has shown the need for Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion to revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries.

The Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion competitions celebrate excellence in imaging, both scientific and artistic in nature. We value the integrity of each image and video selected to appear in our winning galleries, and remain committed to upholding the standards of excellence that have defined this competition.

item.title: PC shipments fall 20.1 percent in “sharpest decline” since Q1 2023
item.description:
“The current decline may be just the beginning of a new downward cycle.”

PC shipments saw a steep drop of about 20 percent in Q3 2026, analysts reported this week.

The industry saw its “sharpest decline since “Q1 2023,” Omdia said in an announcement toady. Global shipments of laptops, desktops, and workstations fell 21.2 percent year over year (YoY) to 58.1 million devices, the analyst said.

Desktop PC shipments (including desktop workstations) decreased 23.5 percent to 11.7 million units, and laptop shipments (including laptop workstations) declined 20.6 percent to 46.4 million, per Omdia.

IDC shared similar findings. The analyst said this week that PC shipments fell 20.1 percent YoY to 62.7 million units, compared to 78.5 million in Q3 2025.

The industry also shipped 9.1 percent fewer PCs in Q3 2026 than it did in Q2 2026, when 68.2 million units shipped, per IDC.

The 20.1 percent YoY decline is the biggest drop that the IDC has ever recorded during a year’s third quarter, the IDC said, perPCMag.

The drop in shipments is also notable considering that Q3 PC shipments usually surpass Q2’s numbers.

“If looking at all quarters, then we have seen other quarters in recent years with larger declines, such as 2022 Q4, which was -28.2 percent, and 2023 Q1, which was -28.7 percent. Both were coming off pandemic highs,” Jitesh Ubrani, research director for consumer devices at IDC, told PCMag.

In its announcement this week, IDC said that many PC vendors and sales channels stocked up on PC shipments earlier in the year in anticipation of memory price hikes. That meant minimal demand remained during Q3.

“[Sales] channels are now worried about carrying too much inventory into a market where high prices are suppressing demand,” Ubrani said in a statement.

“That could translate into promotions and some short-term relief for consumers, but we don’t expect pricing anywhere near what it was a year ago. Prices will remain elevated. With macro conditions worsening, the risk is that the outlook for the next few quarters gets worse before it gets better.”

IDC said that it expects PC prices to decrease “only modestly and briefly.”

Omdia research director Ishan Dutt said the Q3 drop “comes as no surprise.”

“The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly. On the supply side, vendors and their ODM partners began scaling back production in [Q3], while channel partners continued working through elevated inventory levels,” he said in a statement.

Since 2025, surging demand for HBM and server DRAM for AI workloads has led to limited manufacturing capacity for consumer devices, like consumer PCs,smartphones,andgaming consoles. Memoryand storagenowrepresent nearly 40 percent of the bill of materialsfor PC manufacturing, but it’s typically 15 percent, per Ben Yeh, principal analyst at Omdia. Meanwhile, PC prices have increased “more than fourfold,” he said, adding:

Although PC vendors have raised prices multiple times over the past few quarters, these increases have yet to fully offset the impact. These pressures are expected to persist, and the current decline may be just the beginning of a new downward cycle.

Omdia expects PC shipments to decline 24 percent YoY next quarter and then 7 percent in 2027.

Last week, executives from Micron and Samsung indicated the components shortages couldcontinue through 2028.

“Alongside continued increases in memory and storage prices, shortages of processors, graphics cards, and numerous IC components have made supply chain and inventory management more difficult for PC vendors,” Omdia said.
